H1.text: Vinegar tastes sour. Glucose tastes sweet. Formalin keeps lab specimens from rotting.

H2.text: Three very different substances. Yet inside, their atoms come in the very same ratio.

H3.text: Diya spots a puzzle in her kitchen. The glucose packet says C six H twelve O six. Her notes say C H two O.

H4.text: Which one is right? Both are. They are two different kinds of formula.

H5.text: By the end of this video, you will find a formula from nothing but percentages.

P1.text: So what are these two formulas?

P2.text: The empirical formula gives the simplest whole number ratio of atoms in a compound. Empirical means found by experiment.

P3.text: The molecular formula gives the exact number of each kind of atom in one molecule.

P4.text: Glucose has six carbons, twelve hydrogens and six oxygens. That is its molecular formula.

P5.text: Divide every number by six, and you get one, two, one. C H two O. That is its empirical formula.

P6.text: The number we divided by is called n. The molecular formula is n times the empirical formula.

S1.text: Let's watch this on our molecule bench. Here is benzene.

S2.text: Six carbon atoms in a ring, each holding one hydrogen. Every stick is a shared pair of electrons.

S3.text: Count the atoms. Six carbons and six hydrogens. C six H six.

S4.text: Now the bonds open, and we sort the atoms into equal pieces.

S5.text: Six identical pieces. Each piece has one carbon and one hydrogen.

S6.text: So the empirical formula of benzene is C H, and n is six.

S7.text: Now keep just two pieces and join them. Their electrons pair up again, three pairs between the carbons.

S8.text: This is acetylene, the gas burned in welding torches. C two H two. Here n is two.

B1.text: Pause and think. Benzene and acetylene. Do they have the same empirical formula?

B2.text: Yes! Both reduce to C H. Same simplest ratio, but different molecules, so different molecular formulas.

D1.text: Now the real job. A lab gives us only percentages. Glucose is forty percent carbon, six point seven percent hydrogen, and fifty three point three percent oxygen.

D2.text: Step one. Take one hundred grams, so each percent becomes grams. Forty grams of carbon, six point seven of hydrogen, fifty three point three of oxygen.

D3.text: Step two. Turn grams into moles. Divide by the atomic mass. Carbon twelve, hydrogen one, oxygen sixteen.

D4.text: That gives three point three three, six point seven, and three point three three moles.

D5.text: Step three. Divide each by the smallest, three point three three. We get one, two, one. So the empirical formula is C H two O.

D6.text: Step four. Find n. The molar mass of glucose is one hundred eighty grams. C H two O weighs thirty. One eighty divided by thirty is six.

D7.text: Six times C H two O gives C six H twelve O six. The real molecule.

T1.text: Remember this. Empirical is the simplest ratio. Molecular is the real count.

W1.text: Now, the worked example from your NCERT book.

W2.text: A compound has four point zero seven percent hydrogen, twenty four point two seven percent carbon, and seventy one point six five percent chlorine. Its molar mass is ninety eight point nine six grams.

W3.text: In one hundred grams, divide by the atomic masses. Hydrogen gives four point zero four moles. Carbon and chlorine give two point zero two one moles each.

W4.text: Divide by the smallest. Hydrogen two, carbon one, chlorine one. The empirical formula is C H two C L.

W5.text: Its empirical formula mass is forty nine point four eight grams.

W6.text: So n is ninety eight point nine six divided by forty nine point four eight, which is two.

W7.text: Double everything. The molecular formula is C two H four C L two.

X2.text: Say your ratio comes out as one to one point five. Some students round one point five up to two.

X3.text: That is wrong. One point five is not close to a whole number. Multiply every number by two instead. One to one point five becomes two to three.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As a numerical. Percentages and a molar mass are given, and you find both formulas.

Q1.text: Exam level now. An oxide of nitrogen has thirty six point eight percent nitrogen and sixty three point two percent oxygen. Its molar mass is seventy six grams per mole. What is its molecular formula? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. N two O three.

A2.text: Moles first. Thirty six point eight over fourteen is two point six three. Sixty three point two over sixteen is three point nine five.

A3.text: Divide by the smallest. One to one point five. Multiply by two, and you get two to three. So N two O three.

A4.text: Its mass is twenty eight plus forty eight, seventy six. So n is one. Option A rounded one point five up to two.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. What is the empirical formula of hydrogen peroxide, H two O two?

Y3.text: Two. Why must a ratio of one to one point five be multiplied, not rounded?

Y4.text: Three. A compound has the empirical formula C H two and a molar mass of fifty six grams. What is n?

N1.text: Next time: how much oxygen does a gas stove flame really use up? We find out in chemical equations and stoichiometry.
